paras: The expulsion of Tom Clay from Muscatine took place on August 13, 1903, when Clay, a Black man described as a detective, was forced to leave the Iowa town minutes after a murder suspect he had helped identify was cleared. Wire briefs said Clay was "chased out of town," while a fuller Muscatine dispatch said the county attorney, the sheriff and a justice gave him until the next train to leave because local indignation against him was so intense.

On May 14, 1903, Arthur Meade, a young man of West Liberty, Iowa, was shot dead during a holdup in a restaurant there, and Governor Cummins and citizens offered a $1,000 reward for the killer. On August 12 Bert Sheppard, about 22 and the son of a wealthy Oskaloosa coal operator, was arrested in Muscatine on a charge of the murder. The Marshalltown Evening Times-Republican credited the information behind the arrest to Sheriff Andrew Hofer of Johnson County and Iowa City night policeman Mac Burnett, who believed Sheppard matched a man Burnett had seen the night before the murder.

According to the Audubon Republican's Muscatine dispatch, it was Clay who led the two officers to believe their man was in Muscatine and who pointed out Sheppard there, claiming to have other evidence as well. The same dispatch said Clay had just been released from the Johnson county jail after serving a sentence for "crushing a man's skull," and that he had figured as a detective in cases against Muscatine saloonkeepers ten years earlier.

The case against Sheppard collapsed within a day: a Wilton night watchman failed to identify him, and testimony from Bert Jordan of Iowa City showed he did not match the man Burnett had seen. Sheppard was released at his preliminary hearing before a Muscatine justice on August 13, the evidence being judged insufficient. About fifteen minutes later, by the Audubon Republican's account, County Attorney Ingham, Sheriff Sweart and Justice Eversmeyer called Clay in and gave him until the next train to leave town, and he left. A special to the Times-Republican, dated the same day, reported only that Clay "was chased out of town today after Sheppard was found innocent," without saying by whom.
Sheppard also left Muscatine, and it was believed he had not returned to Oskaloosa. The coverage gives no later word of Clay's whereabouts and reports no protest or official inquiry into his removal.

The expulsion surfaced in three white newspapers, all as short items appended to the larger story of a millionaire's son wrongly arrested for murder. The Times-Republican ran it on its front page on August 13 under the headline "Negro Chased Out of Town," and the Bemidji Daily Pioneer in Minnesota printed nearly the same text on August 15 as "Accuser Chased Out of Town," with "today" changed to "yesterday." The Audubon Republican's longer report, published August 20, cast the order as the officials' answer to public indignation and recounted Clay's jail term, framing him as the source of the trouble.

Coverage of the arrest itself centered on Sheppard, his wealthy family and his protests of innocence. The Rock Island Argus, writing for readers who knew the Sheppard family, headed its story "Misapprehension Leads to Arrest of Bert Sheppard" and blamed the arrest on "the statement of a negro who has a reputation for being unreliable," without naming Clay or mentioning his expulsion. Other papers, such as the Beatrice Daily Express and the Cresco Twice-a-Week Plain Dealer, reported Sheppard's release without mentioning Clay at all, and no Black newspaper account of the episode appears in the coverage.

The two independent accounts differ on who drove Clay out: the wire version says only that he was chased, while the Muscatine dispatch printed in Audubon names three county officials who ordered him to take the next train. The Bemidji reprint's "yesterday" under an August 15 dateline would put the expulsion on August 14, but the earlier Times-Republican special and the Audubon dispatch both place it on August 13.
